 MILTON, Fla. -- Debris removal in Milton is now expected to cost far more than city leaders first projected, as residents continue clearing storm damage nearly two weeks after a hurricane tore through the area.
 City officials now estimate debris removal will cost about $25 million. Last week, officials put the price tag at around $16 million.
 Milton resident Mitchell Burt is still working to clear his property and said he did not anticipate the storm’s impact.
 “I do what you're supposed to do but I do wish we maybe boarded up. The windows held. The trees were definitely the real threat with this one,” Burt said.
 Burt still has a tree on his roof, one example of widespread damage across the city. Milton officials said more than half of the buildings in town have some type of damage, and about 5% are unlivable.
 As residents rebuild, Mayor Heather Lindsay urged people to follow building codes and avoid cutting corners.
 “You don't want to try to save money by being your own electrician and accidentally set your home on fire. You don't want your neighbor to install a fence without a qualified contractor, and that fence be destroyed in the next storm with debris coming through the bedroom window of your child. The rules are in place for a reason, your safety and your neighbor's safety,” Lindsay said.
 Officials estimate there are about 400,000 cubic yards of vegetative debris throughout the city, along with another 35,000 cubic yards of construction debris. Clearing and processing that material is expected to cost $25 million, which the city said is about a third of Milton’s operating budget.
 Lindsay said residents will ultimately bear part of the cost even if the city receives state and federal reimbursement.
 “We pay it and then we apply for reimbursement. And the state and the federal resources that may become available to us will reimburse most of it but I believe only up to 75%. So it's 25% will still come out of the taxpayers' pockets right here in Milton,” she said.
 The recovery is also reshaping Milton’s holiday plans. Lindsay said the city will not be able to support the Veterans Day parade, Light Up Milton or the Christmas parade this year because police, fire and public works crews need to stay focused on recovery efforts.
 “We're going to be scrutinized for everything we do that is not essential, so we're trying to be mindful of our duty to all taxpayers to be as be efficient and focus on essential services,” Lindsay said.
 As of Tuesday, the city had collected nearly 100,000 cubic yards of vegetative debris, though the mayor said crews have not finished their first pass through the city.
 Burt said he sees the debris trucks working daily and expects they will reach his neighborhood when they can.
 “I see the big trucks go by every day you know they're shipping stuff right over there. I know they're gonna get to me. They just they have their route they take. We've got everything we need here our road works. I just need some more space soon for some more trash you know to pile up,” he said.
 Milton officials said 40 debris haulers are working seven days a week. They expect debris removal will continue into November and possibly December.
